The church of the Republic of Venice, at the east end of Piazza San Marco and joined to the Doge's Palace. It was built to hold the body of Saint Mark, which two Venetian merchants carried off from Alexandria in 828 or 829. Until the fall of the republic in 1797 it was the doge's own chapel, a shrine of the state rather than the seat of a bishop; it became the cathedral of Venice only in 1807.

The present building is the third on the site, begun probably in 1063 under Doge Domenico Contarini and dedicated in 1094. Like the two earlier churches it follows the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople: a cross-shaped plan with five domes, stretched along its length for state processions. The domes, vaults and upper walls are covered in mosaics on a gold ground, made and remade over some eight hundred years, some of them from drawings by Titian and Tintoretto. The Pala d'Oro, a golden altarpiece ordered from Constantinople in 1102, stands on the high altar.

The plain brick church was dressed in marble mostly in the 13th century, much of it loot from the Fourth Crusade and the sack of Constantinople in 1204: columns, carved reliefs, the porphyry Tetrarchs and the four bronze horses from the Hippodrome, set over the main door. Napoleon took the horses to Paris in 1797; they came back in 1815, and since 1974 the originals have stood inside, with copies outside. The tall outer domes were added in the 13th century and the Gothic crest of the front around 1400.
